beats.say: Cut a strip of paper in half just thirty one times, and you're down to the size of an atom.
Start with eleven inches. Cut it in half, keep one piece, repeat. Six cuts: four point four millimeters.
Nine cuts: about half a millimeter. And you're not even a third of the way there.
Twelve cuts: thinner than a human hair.
Sixteen: smaller than a red blood cell.
Twenty two: smaller than a flu virus.
Twenty eight: narrower than a strand of DNA.
Thirty one cuts: about the size of a single atom.
But an atom is mostly empty space. To get all the way down to a carbon nucleus at its center, you'd need fifteen more cuts. Forty six in total.
Follow Ship With Pip for more.

title: Cut paper in half 31 times and you reach an atom
caption: Start with a strip of US Letter paper, 11 inches (279.4 mm) long. Cut it in half and keep one piece. 6 cuts: 4.4 mm. 9 cuts: 0.55 mm. 12 cuts: 68.2 µm, thinner than a human hair (about 75 µm). 16 cuts: 4.3 µm, smaller than a red blood cell (about 7.7 µm). 22 cuts: 66.6 nm, smaller than a flu virus (about 100 nm). 28 cuts: 1.04 nm, narrower than DNA (2 nm). 31 cuts: 0.13 nm, about the size of an atom (radius 1 to 2 Ångström). And the atom is mostly empty: a carbon nucleus is about 4 femtometres across, which takes 46 cuts, 15 more. That's exponential shrinking: 1 over 2 to the power of 31.
facts: start 0.2794 m (11 in), factor 0.5. cut n = first n with 0.2794/2^n below landmark: hair 75 um (PBS: hair about 75,000 nm) -> 12 (68.2 um); RBC 7.7 um (BioNumbers 108239) -> 16 (4.26 um); flu 100 nm (PBS/HHMI) -> 22 (66.6 nm); DNA 2 nm (Lancaster glossary) -> 28 (1.04 nm); atom: Britannica radius 1-2 A, so diameter >= 2e-10 m -> 31 (0.130 nm); carbon nucleus about 4 fm (Britannica) -> 46 (3.97 fm); 46-31 = 15. 6 cuts = 4.37 mm. 9 cuts = 0.546 mm; 9 < 31/3.
